title: From the City payroll to the other side of the table
question: Who left a City job and, within three years, was lobbying their old department, steering permits through it, or running an organization it funds?
finding: Of 12,109 people with testable names who left the payroll between fiscal 2017 and 2025, 11 share a name with a registered lobbyist active afterwards and 5 of those reported contacts with the very department that had paid them: 0 inside the one-year ban on the dates available, 0 too close to call, and 2 whose first contact came within two months after the year ran out. 1 became a paid permit consultant, and 11 turn up at an organization their former department funds: 6 as a paid officer or employee, 1 as an outside contractor and 4 on the board without pay.
how: Names are matched only when they behave as one person in the City payroll and are rare (fewer than one other Bay Area resident expected to share the name, from how common each first and last name is among 71,958 City employees; names held by two or more licensed California health providers are dropped). 48,514 of 68,293 payroll names pass. The payroll file names employees only from fiscal 2017. A row appears only with a second link: lobbying contacts or permit work with the former department itself, or City money from that department to the organization (at least $100,000 around the move). Unpaid board seats are listed only for people who held a management, policy or Form 700 position. “Left” means the last fiscal year with at least $15,000 of pay; where the person filed a Form 700 leaving-office statement its exact date is used.
limits: A shared name is not proof of identity. The City’s rules are narrower than “never”: for one year a former employee may not lobby the former department for someone else; permanently they may not work on a particular matter they handled; and for a year they may not be paid by a contractor whose contract they personally helped award, unless the Ethics Commission grants a waiver. Whether a person handled a given contract is not in any public file. Tax returns on file begin with tax year 2020, so for people who left before then a board seat may be older than their departure. The exact leaving date is known only where a Form 700 gives it; otherwise it is estimated from the hours paid in the final fiscal year, which can be off by months when someone worked part-time or was paid out leave.
